column3: The immediate continuation extends his false supposition from the garden's permanence to denial of the Hour and an assumed better return.
The unalterable revealed word stands over against the owner's unsupported personal prediction.
Its permanent loss of success after coerced return is a distant contrast to the owner's claim that his present condition will never end.
It directly names a manifest wrongdoer against himself, clarifying the focus's self-wronging as a moral condition.
Granted everlasting abiding supplies the proper counterpart to the owner's self-asserted permanence.
God-granted eternal reward contrasts with the owner's unfounded claim that a worldly garden cannot perish.
A display of possession is identified as the Lord's favor and a test of gratitude, correcting the owner's possessive confidence.
Its warning against seeking worldly adornment frames the parable's garden as a test of the gaze and desire.
The refusal to wish for death because of prior wrongdoing has only a broad connection through wrongful action and an absolute claim.
It distinguishes the one who wrongs himself from more rightly directed servants, making that focus description morally substantive.
The companion directly corrects the owner at his garden: he should have attributed its existence and power to God.
The hypocrites' false promise of never obeying anyone is another unreliable absolute assertion, though in a different setting.
Moses entering the city and the ensuing conflict do not clarify the garden owner's self-wronging or permanence claim.
The nearby declaration of truth, belief, disbelief, and punishment supplies the moral horizon for the owner's speech.
It portrays a false prediction that something will never happen, illuminating the owner's confident but baseless forecast.
Striving benefits oneself, but the ayah does not materially specify the focus's wealth, permanence, or self-deception.
After the garden's loss, the owner has neither a supporting group nor power to rescue himself, disproving his confidence.
Divinely decreed everlasting punishment contrasts with the owner's imagined permanence for a worldly possession.
It closely repeats the pattern of receiving favor, claiming it as one's own, denying the Hour, and presuming a better return.
The next ayah contrasts the owner's self-deluding claim with God's preservation of the reward for genuine good action.
Eternal gardens are promised to faithful righteous people, distinguishing granted abiding from possessive presumption.
The destruction of a crop belonging to people who wrong themselves gives a close material image for the focus's vulnerable garden.
The local contrast supplies gardens of lasting reward rather than a worldly garden mistakenly thought indestructible.
The permanent exclusion of false accusers from testimony is a legal ruling unrelated to the focus's claim about his garden.
The ruined town and God's power over death challenge any inference that an apparent material state is beyond reversal.
It depicts people whose worldly effort is lost while they suppose it excellent, closely paralleling false self-assessment.
Faithful action is followed by God-granted everlasting gardens and provision, contrasting with the owner's temporal possession.
Thankfulness for received wisdom benefits the person, providing the fitting response absent from the garden owner's speech.
It begins the two-garden parable and establishes the setting in which the owner's claim is made.
Everlasting punishment for disobedience is only a broad contrast to the owner's asserted permanence.
The believers reject a ruler's temporary worldly power, reinforcing that this worldly life is not the lasting measure.
The lasting abode whose inhabitants seek no change sharply contrasts with the owner's unfounded claim for his garden.
It presents enduring gardens as reward granted by the Lord to those who fear Him, not as a possession secured by wealth.
Entering prison and the prisoners' dreams do not clarify the focus's central themes.
The full productivity and flowing river explain why the owner could mistake a prosperous garden for a permanent one.
It repeats the fear-driven refusal to wish for death, with only a broad link through wrongdoing and absolute language.
The distinction between recompense for evil and entry into the garden for believing righteous action corrects presumptive entitlement.
Gardens of Firdaws are prepared lodging for faith and righteous action, contrasting with a transient garden claimed as permanent.
God's true promise of eternal gardens provides a direct contrast to the owner's unsupported claim about worldly permanence.
The owner's boast of greater wealth and stronger followers supplies the social arrogance immediately behind his claim.
Revelation increasing believers in faith does not closely illuminate the owner's garden, beyond a general contrast in response to signs.
The warning against taking servants as protectors besides God anticipates the parable's exposure of misplaced reliance.
Its use of supposition occurs in a different confrontation and provides little beyond the verbal form of the owner's claim.
The companion identifies the owner's stance as disbelief in the Creator, giving the theological diagnosis of the focus.
Entry into the garden follows faith and righteous deeds without injustice, not material advantage or self-assurance.
The parable concludes that true authority, reward, and outcome belong to God alone, overturning the owner's confidence.
The call to shared belief and notice of dissension do not materially clarify the garden owner's claim.
The companion's exclusive devotion to God directly counters the owner's failure to acknowledge his Lord.
The brother's decision to remain under a pledge is narratively and thematically remote from the focus.
The garden's actual ruin and the owner's regret realize the destruction he had declared impossible.
Turning from the Lord's signs while forgetting prior deeds describes a wider pattern of self-wronging and persistent misguidance.
The companion explicitly foresees the garden being reduced to barren, slippery ground, refuting the owner's permanence claim.
People's confidence in favorable passage collapses under danger, showing how secure appearances can be suddenly overturned.
The possible disappearance of the garden's water exposes a basic resource as beyond the owner's control or recovery.
Unequal worldly rank and what people are given are presented as a divine test, not evidence of secure ownership.
Those who desire worldly life envy Qarun's visible splendor, paralleling the valuation that makes the garden persuasive.
The end of Moses's companionship concerns patience with hidden wisdom, not the owner's garden or claim of permanence.
Demanding that a messenger possess a treasure or productive garden treats worldly wealth as proof of standing, a related false measure.
The rhetorical challenge to presumptuous hopes of entering bliss parallels confidence in a favorable outcome without its grounds.
The question about devotion to idols is too general to materially clarify the focus's garden and permanence claim.
The prohibition on worshipping Satan identifies misplaced obedience as an enemy-led path, broadly related to self-wronging.
The hoopoe's report of certain news has no substantive connection to the focus.
Moses explicitly acknowledges that he wronged himself and seeks forgiveness, offering a repentant contrast to the owner's self-wronging.
Satan's lure of immortality through the forbidden tree closely parallels being seduced by a promise of unending possession.
A mistaken supposition about whether people and jinn would lie about God has only a general link through false assumption.
The command never to repeat slander is a specific ethical ruling unrelated to the focus.
The Israelites' refusal ever to enter the land is a different absolute claim driven by fear, with little thematic overlap.
The command to enter Paradise provides a distant contrast between the true garden granted after faith and the owner's worldly garden.
The queen's corrected perception and confession of self-wronging offer only an indirect parallel.
The God-fearing are admitted to the garden to abide, showing the source and recipients of true enduring residence.
It calls associating partners with God a great wrongdoing, clarifying the gravity later exposed in the owner's stance.
The evidentiary test in Joseph's story does not clarify the focus.
Worship is due to the Lord who owns everything, directly challenging the owner's implicit treatment of the garden as autonomous possession.
Entry into God's garden is a distant but relevant contrast to the owner's temporal garden.
The prohibition on standing at a particular mosque forever is unrelated to the owner's material claim of permanence.
Wrongdoing, recognition of testing, and repentance provide a broad moral contrast to the owner's unrepentant self-wronging.
The allocation of water to the she-camel and people has no material connection to the focus.
The sleepers' uncertainty about elapsed time does not clarify the owner's confidence about his garden's future.
It explicitly calls worldly life a deceptive enjoyment and redirects success to the final garden, opposing the owner's temporal horizon.
The messenger's refusal of payment does not illuminate the focus.
The great success is faith, forgiven wrongs, and God-granted eternal gardens, not confidence in present wealth.
Truthfulness is rewarded with eternal gardens, contrasting divine reward with the owner's self-serving assertion.
Repentance, faith, and righteous action lead to the garden, but the connection to the focus is general.
An unsupported claim of exclusive entry into Paradise parallels the owner's unsupported assertion about an assured outcome.
The brief description of one who fears God does not sufficiently clarify the focus.
The idolaters' momentary admission that they are wrongdoers is only a broad parallel to self-wronging.
It holds together good in this world, the hereafter, repentance, and divine mercy, correcting a purely worldly horizon.
Pharaoh's insult to Moses does not clarify the focus.
Believers being required to assume good of one another concerns slander, not the owner's false supposition.
The righteous enter Paradise because of what they did, contrasting moral recompense with the owner's confidence in possessions.
Its response to blessings is gratitude, righteous action, and repentance, providing a constructive contrast to the owner's ingratitude.
God's creation and governance of all things deny any independent permanence to the owner's garden.
The address to disbelievers alone does not clarify the focus.
The regret of followers and leaders after punishment gives only a distant consequence parallel to the owner's later regret.
Punishment for persecuting believers does not materially clarify the focus.
Material benefits and adornment from the sea invite gratitude, but the connection to the garden owner is indirect.
The call to Abraham has no substantive connection to the focus.
The report of earlier peoples rejecting their messengers supplies only a broad backdrop of disbelief.
The prohibition on wronging yourselves supports the moral wording but not the focus's specific garden claim.
Inheritance shares and debt provisions do not clarify the garden owner's self-wronging or false permanence claim.
The worldly life is made attractive to disbelievers, explaining how visible prosperity can be mistaken for true worth.
A flourishing garden can be reduced by destructive wind and fire, directly challenging confidence in a garden's immunity from loss.
The attraction of wealth, children, livestock, and cultivated land is named as worldly enjoyment rather than the lasting destination.
Neither wealth nor children can avail their possessors before God, limiting the security the owner reads from possession.
Adam and his wife acknowledge that they wronged themselves and seek mercy, providing a repentant contrast to the owner's self-wronging.
Wealth and children are explicitly a trial, supplying the evaluative frame for the owner's garden and social strength.
When family, wealth, trade, and dwellings are loved above God, their apparent value becomes spiritually destructive.
Wealth and children are not necessarily favor; they can be the means of distress in worldly life and punishment beyond it.
The repetition that wealth and children are a trial reinforces that abundance cannot demonstrate a secure outcome.
The life of this world is compared to vegetation that flourishes and is then suddenly reduced to stubble, closely matching the garden's vulnerability.
Those who seek only worldly life and its adornment receive its temporary return but lose their lasting share.
Preferring worldly life over the Hereafter diagnoses the distorted valuation behind treating a garden as the final horizon.
A secure and well-provided town is made to taste hunger and fear after ingratitude, showing prosperity can be withdrawn.
Whoever wants only the immediate world receives a limited allotment and then faces the Hereafter, opposing the owner's narrowed time horizon.
When human beings receive favor they turn away arrogantly, a behavioral parallel to the owner's response to abundance.
Earthly adornment is explicitly made a test of who acts best, framing the garden's beauty as examination rather than permanence.
The parable of rain-fed vegetation becoming dry debris gives the chapter's direct general image for worldly transience.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and hope; it states the parable's governing contrast.
Worldly splendor given to others is a test and must not draw the eye away from the Lord's better and more lasting provision.
Every soul will taste death and both evil and good are tests, denying a horizon of unqualified worldly continuity.
Wealth and children should not be read as proof that God is hastening good to their possessors.
The correction continues: those surrounded by wealth and children do not perceive the real meaning of that provision.
Deeds that look like water to the thirsty but prove empty provide a related image of deceptive appearances and failed expectation.
Building as though one will live forever parallels the owner's attempt to project permanence from present material strength.
The Day when wealth and children do not benefit directly overturns the owner's reliance on property and social standing.
Only a sound heart benefits on that Day, supplying the moral alternative to possessions as security.
Whatever worldly goods are given are only enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting.
Qarun's exultant dependence on his great stores closely parallels the garden owner's confidence in accumulated wealth.
Qarun attributes his wealth to his own knowledge, a close counterpart to treating a received garden as self-secured.
The earth swallowing Qarun and his house demonstrates the abrupt defeat of material security and social self-rescue.
Observers learn that God expands and restricts provision, correcting their earlier wish for Qarun's worldly position.
Worldly life is diversion and play, while the real life is the final abode; this directly corrects the owner's temporal valuation.
The worldly life and the deceiver must not mislead people about God, a direct warning against false security.
Affluent elites commonly reject warning, providing a social pattern into which the garden owner's self-assurance fits.
The claim that wealth and children guarantee immunity from punishment closely matches the owner's material confidence.
Wealth and children do not bring a person near to God; faith and righteous action, not possession, determine recompense.
The worldly life is not to deceive people about God, identifying the general error embodied by the owner's prediction.
Attachment to splendid possessions can make one neglect remembrance of the Lord, a related failure of valuation.
Water produces thriving crops that later wither and become debris, another explicit image of the garden's impermanence.
After receiving favor, a person claims it was given because of personal knowledge, paralleling possessive self-deception.
Worldly life is only temporary enjoyment while the Hereafter is the permanent home, directly negating the owner's horizon.
When given favor, people turn away arrogantly; this closely describes the owner's posture within abundance.
Whatever people receive is only enjoyment of worldly life, whereas what is with God is better and more lasting.
Even lavish houses and material display are described as mere enjoyment of worldly life, not lasting distinction.
Ornaments and visible luxury continue the argument that worldly splendor is not evidence of final favor.
All such adornment is worldly enjoyment, while the Hereafter belongs to the God-conscious.
Those who exhausted their good things in worldly life are confronted with the failure of that worldly valuation.
Worldly life is play and diversion, and wealth is tested rather than held out as a permanent possession.
Worldly life is adornment, rivalry in wealth and children, and vegetation that later becomes debris; it is a comprehensive parallel to the focus.
People are told not to exult over what they receive, directly opposing the owner's boastful confidence.
Protection from one's own greed is the mark of success, supplying a moral contrast to possessive attachment.
Wealth and children must not distract from God's remembrance, naming the spiritual danger of abundance.
Wealth and children are a trial, again denying that their presence proves stability or favor.
The owners of the garden are tested through a garden that is later devastated, making this a close narrative counterpart.
After the garden's loss, its owners hope their Lord will replace it with better, the opposite of claiming the present garden cannot perish.
Wealth is confessed not to have availed its possessor, reducing material accumulation to failed security.
Abundant wealth is listed among gifts bestowed on a person who nevertheless resists gratitude and warning.
Despite extensive gifts, the person still demands more, exposing acquisitiveness rather than secure sufficiency.
Love of the immediate world is contrasted with neglect of the Hereafter, directly naming the focus's shortened horizon.
Those who love the immediate world leave behind a weighty Day, another direct contrast to the owner's outlook.
Transgression and preference for worldly life are given as a path with a final consequence, clarifying the moral stakes of the focus.
The resulting destination is contrasted with worldly preference, redirecting the claim of lasting security to the final abode.
Preferring worldly life is explicitly rebuked, matching the owner's valuation of present possession.
The Hereafter is declared better and more lasting, providing the direct correction to asserted worldly permanence.
A person mistakes expanded provision for honor, the same faulty inference from material abundance.
Intense love of wealth identifies the desire that can make material abundance appear decisive.
The self-sufficient person who denies the better outcome provides a broader portrait of the owner's posture.
Human beings transgress when they see themselves as self-sufficient, closely diagnosing the owner's confidence.
Seeing oneself as self-sufficient is the stated cause of that transgression, directly relevant to self-wronging through possession.
Intense love of wealth describes the attachment that makes a garden appear to guarantee the future.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts people, directly challenging the owner's boast in wealth and followers.
That rivalry lasts only until the graves, cutting off the imagined permanence of accumulated worldly goods.
The hoarder and counter of wealth is a close moral parallel to possessive confidence in material accumulation.
He thinks his wealth will make him immortal, the Qur'an's closest verbal and conceptual counterpart to the owner's claim.
Abu Lahab's wealth and gains do not avail him, providing a concise outcome-based rejection of material security.
